name: CPython
summary: A Python runtime organized around interpreters and thread states, execution frames for code blocks, dynamic name binding, and a reference-managed object and C extension boundary.

features.name: Interpreter and thread-state hierarchy
features.description: The Python runtime model distinguishes global runtime state, interpreters, and thread states. An interpreter encapsulates non-process-global runtime state, while each thread state is tied to one interpreter and one host thread.
benefits: Provides a reusable boundary for runtime state and execution context
Allows multiple interpreters and thread states to be reasoned about separately
costs: Shared interpreter resources require coordination across host threads
State ownership and thread affinity add embedding complexity

features.name: Execution frames and dynamic name binding
features.description: Python code blocks execute in execution frames, and names refer to objects through binding and scope-resolution rules. Dynamic features such as eval and exec can supply or alter namespaces at runtime.
benefits: Supports a flexible object and module programming model
Makes execution context available for debugging and dynamic evaluation
costs: Runtime name resolution limits some static optimization opportunities
Dynamic namespace mutation can make behavior harder to predict

features.name: Reference-managed object and C API boundary
features.description: The CPython C API exposes strong-reference operations such as Py_INCREF, Py_DECREF, and Py_NewRef. Releasing the last strong reference invokes the object's deallocation function, which can execute arbitrary Python code.
benefits: Provides explicit lifetime operations for native extensions and embedding
Allows objects to be reclaimed when their strong-reference count reaches zero
costs: Extension code must obey reference ownership rules
Deallocation can re-enter Python and therefore requires consistent object state

mathematical_views.question: How do runtime, interpreter, thread-state, and execution-frame entities evolve as Python code runs?
assumptions: The documented runtime layers are modeled as state components rather than literal implementation objects
Thread affinity and interpreter ownership are transition preconditions
The view abstracts host scheduler behavior and platform-specific internals

mathematical_views.question: How do strong references and deallocation transitions govern the lifetime of Python objects exposed through the C API?
assumptions: Objects are vertices and strong references are counted ownership edges
A zero strong-reference count permits a deallocation transition under the documented rules
Immortal objects, cyclic garbage collection, and implementation-specific optimizations are outside this simplified view

benefits: Explicit runtime isolation and execution ownership boundaries
costs: Embedding and concurrency require coordination across nested state

benefits: Flexible introspection, modules, and dynamic evaluation
costs: Dynamic lookup and mutation complicate static reasoning and optimization

benefits: Direct, interoperable lifetime control for native extensions
costs: Reference mistakes and re-entrant deallocation can cause correctness failures
